title: Wood Mackenzie Mid-Year Outlook: oil and gas industry cash-rich but capital-cautious as nearly half a trillion-dollar windfall fails to trigger a spending surge
gist: Wood Mackenzie's mid-year outlook finds the global upstream sector on track for a $495bn cash windfall in 2026 as Brent averages ~$91/bbl versus $60/bbl planning assumptions, yet the 49 largest IOCs/NOCs have kept capex flat and buybacks are forecast down ~5% YoY, choosing to hoard cash and deleverage rather than spend, even as M&A activity (Shell/ARC, Devon/Coterra, Mitsubishi/Aethon) hit a two-year high and a steep production-decline problem looms into the 2030s.

insights.claim: The global upstream oil and gas sector could accumulate a cash windfall of US$495 billion in 2026 if Brent averages US$90 per barrel, more than double the cash flow expected under initial planning assumptions of around US$60 per barrel.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A near-$500bn windfall versus budget is a major balance-sheet tailwind for upstream operators that has not yet shown up as increased shareholder returns or investment — watch H2 for whether it gets deployed.
insights.quote: the global upstream sector could accumulate a cash windfall of US$495 billion this year, assuming Brent prices average US$90 per barrel, more than double cash flow expectations based on initial planning assumptions of around US$60 per barrel
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie's mid-year upstream and corporate outlook

insights.claim: The 49 largest IOCs and NOCs in Wood Mackenzie's corporate coverage are set to net US$272 billion of the 2026 windfall, equivalent to 70% of their combined investment budget for the year, yet those investment budgets remain flat.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Windfall cash equal to 70% of annual capex sitting idle signals major optionality for future buybacks, M&A or investment surprises among large-cap oil and gas names.
insights.quote: The 49 largest IOCs and NOCs in Wood Mackenzie's corporate coverage net US$272 billion of this, which is equivalent to 70% of their combined investment for the year.

insights.claim: Despite dated Brent averaging US$91 per barrel through H1 2026 versus a US$60 planning assumption, capital budgets across the 49 largest IOCs and NOCs have barely moved and shareholder return frameworks have been broadly maintained.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Confirms a structural shift toward capital discipline in the oil majors/NOCs — investors should not expect capex to track oil price upside 1:1 as it did in past cycles.
insights.quote: With dated Brent prices averaging US$91 per barrel through H1, capital budgets have barely moved.
insights.locator: Companies entered the year expecting Brent crude to average around US$60

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie forecasts buybacks for its 49-company peer group will fall around 5% year-on-year in 2026, based on plans announced ahead of Q2 reporting, even as cash flow roughly doubled versus plan.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A falling buyback trajectory despite a cash windfall is a contrarian signal versus consensus expectations of aggressive capital returns in a high oil-price environment.
insights.quote: Wood Mackenzie forecasts buybacks for the peer group will be down around 5% year-on-year in 2026, based on announced plans ahead of the Q2 reporting season.
insights.locator: Companies have broadly maintained their original shareholder return frameworks

insights.claim: Tom Ellacott, Wood Mackenzie's Senior VP of Corporate Research, argues that oil and gas companies have largely taken a wait-and-see approach to 2026's macro turmoil, preferring to build cash reserves over returning capital to shareholders or raising investment, and that capital discipline proved more durable than either bulls or bears expected.
insights.speaker: Tom Ellacott
insights.so_what: A senior industry analyst is flagging that neither the bullish (spend/return more) nor bearish (retrench) narrative played out — the base case for 2026 is corporate caution, useful for calibrating sector return expectations.
insights.quote: Capital discipline has proved more durable than either the bears or bulls expected.
insights.locator: What is perhaps most telling about the corporate response

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's Tom Ellacott frames the second half of 2026 as the period that will reveal whether oil and gas companies' strategic response catches up with their financial firepower, since high prices ease financial pressure but do not resolve the industry's next-decade production challenge.
insights.speaker: Tom Ellacott
insights.so_what: Sets a concrete near-term catalyst window (H2 2026) for whether the sector shifts from cash hoarding to deployment.
insights.quote: High prices ease the financial pressure. They do not solve the next-decade production challenge. The second half of 2026 will show whether the strategic response catches up with the financial firepower.
insights.locator: High prices ease the financial pressure

insights.claim: 155 companies tracked by Wood Mackenzie face an average 30% production decline between 2030 and 2040, equivalent to about 32 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, excluding Middle Eastern NOCs.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A 32 million boe/d decline across the tracked peer group by 2040 is a structural reserve-replacement problem that current flat capex budgets are not addressing — a long-horizon watch item for portfolio renewal and M&A activity.
insights.quote: 155 companies tracked by Wood Mackenzie face an average 30% production decline between 2030 and 2040, equivalent to 32 million boe per day
insights.locator: The next-decade production challenge is immense

insights.claim: More than 70 of the 155 companies Wood Mackenzie tracks face production declines of 50% or more by 2040.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Nearly half the tracked peer group faces existential-scale production erosion, raising the odds of further consolidation or aggressive portfolio renewal among mid-size operators.
insights.quote: Over 70 face declines of 50% or more out to 2040.
insights.locator: The next-decade production challenge is immense

insights.claim: Global upstream development spend is on course for a second consecutive year of slight decline in 2026, as operators prioritize maintenance deferral, optimization and low-capital activities over new major project commitments even while enjoying near-term price upside.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Two straight years of declining development spend despite high prices implies underinvestment risk that could tighten future oil and gas supply, a medium-term bullish factor for prices.
insights.quote: Global upstream development spend is on course for a second consecutive year of slight decline.
insights.locator: Capex discipline is holding, but corporate resolve could be tested

insights.claim: Most of Wood Mackenzie's tracked oil and gas peer group has accumulated rather than deployed its 2026 cash windfall, with elevated prices accelerating deleveraging for more leveraged operators.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Faster deleveraging among the more indebted operators reduces sector-wide credit risk and could set up stronger balance sheets for a later wave of buybacks or M&A.
insights.quote: The cash is staying on the balance sheet. Most of the peer group has accumulated rather than deployed its windfall, with elevated prices accelerating deleveraging for more leveraged operators.
insights.locator: The cash is staying on the balance sheet

insights.claim: Despite oil price volatility and broader capital caution, H1 2026 upstream oil and gas M&A deal spend reached its highest total in two years.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: M&A, not capex or buybacks, is the channel where oil and gas companies are actually deploying the cash windfall — a signal to watch for further consolidation targets.
insights.quote: Despite price volatility, H1 deal spend reached its highest total in two years.

insights.claim: Shell acquired ARC for US$16 billion, Devon merged with Coterra in a US$25 billion deal, and Mitsubishi acquired Aethon for US$7.5 billion, among the defining upstream M&A transactions of H1 2026.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: These three deals ($48.5bn combined) illustrate that even in a capex-cautious environment, majors and trading houses are willing to pay up for scale and reserves via consolidation rather than organic investment.
insights.quote: Shell's US$16 billion acquisition of ARC, Devon's US$25 billion merger with Coterra and Mitsubishi's US$7.5 billion acquisition of Aethon were among the defining transactions.

themes.theme: Supply shock from Middle East conflict

insights.claim: Global oil output is expected to be down at least 3% in 2026, a sharp reversal from an earlier forecast increase of similar magnitude, though Wood Mackenzie flags these estimates as tentative given ongoing conflicts.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A swing from +3% expected growth to -3% actual output is a major unplanned supply shock underpinning the 2026 price surge and windfall — a key variable to track for oil price direction.
insights.quote: Oil output is expected to be down at least 3% in 2026, against a forecast increase of similar magnitude.
insights.locator: The global supply picture has deteriorated sharply

insights.claim: Iraq has been the hardest-hit country in the Middle East supply disruption, with up to around 3 million barrels per day of production offline.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: 3 million bpd offline from a single country is roughly 3% of global oil supply — a concrete figure to monitor for de-escalation or further disruption risk.
insights.quote: In the Middle East, Iraq has been hardest hit, with up to around 3 million barrels per day offline.
insights.locator: The global supply picture has deteriorated sharply

insights.claim: Global LNG supply is expected to be down at least 2% in 2026, versus an earlier forecast rise of 8%, with Qatar bearing the brunt of the shortfall.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A 10-point swing in LNG supply expectations (from +8% to -2%) signals tightening global gas markets, relevant for LNG buyers and gas price forecasts.
insights.quote: Global LNG supply will be down at least 2%, against an earlier forecast rise of 8%, with Qatar taking the hit.
insights.locator: The global supply picture has deteriorated sharply

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie expects the Middle East to remain central to the long-term portfolio plans of the world's largest oil and gas operators despite near-term disruption, since no other region matches its scale and cost advantage.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Near-term supply outages in the Middle East are viewed as disruption rather than structural decline — majors are expected to keep prioritizing the region for future portfolio renewal.
insights.quote: Despite near-term disruption, no region matches it for scale and cost advantage.
insights.locator: The Middle East remains critical for portfolio renewal

themes.theme: A geopolitical price cycle, not a demand cycle

insights.claim: Fraser McKay, Head of Upstream Analysis at Wood Mackenzie, argues the 2026 price surge reflects geopolitical conflict rather than underlying demand growth, and that companies are well aware of this distinction when setting capital plans.
insights.speaker: Fraser McKay
insights.so_what: Because operators view the price spike as geopolitically driven rather than demand-driven, they are treating it as less durable, explaining why capex hasn't chased the windfall.
insights.quote: This is not a natural commodity cycle. The price surge reflects geopolitical conflict, not underlying demand, and companies are well aware of it.
insights.locator: This is not a natural commodity cycle

insights.claim: Fraser McKay predicts that if oil prices hold through the second half of 2026, pressure on oil and gas companies to deploy capital via buybacks, M&A or new investment will intensify, and how boards navigate that tension will shape the industry's strategic direction into 2027.
insights.speaker: Fraser McKay
insights.so_what: Flags H2 2026 through 2027 as the window where sustained high prices could force a shift from cash hoarding to active capital deployment — watch for buyback/M&A/capex announcements as the signal.
insights.quote: If prices hold through H2, the pressure to deploy capital via buybacks, M&A or new investment will intensify. How boards navigate that tension will shape the industry's strategic direction into 2027.
insights.locator: Balance sheets are stronger than they have been in years
